candidates.excerpt: operational state of a modern large language model. It can generate highquality text, yet it stalls when asked to navigate a dynamic multi-step workflow in the physical world. The problem lies in the core logic of token prediction. A language model predicts the next word in a sequence. But once that specific task is over, it has no persistent mechanism to hold on to context. It cannot adapt to unexpected friction because it cannot remember the obstacles it faced 10 seconds ago. This is the difference between an engine and a vehicle. The language model provides the raw power, but autonomy requires a chassis, steering, and active sensors to read the road. Simply feeding these engines more data will not result in a self-driving system. Achieving true autonomy requires a structural rebuild of how these systems are built from the ground up. Computer scientists are moving away from the isolated monolith. Instead, they are surrounding the core language model with specialized cognitive modules that manage specific tasks like memory and planning. This integrated architecture is called a foundation agent. As the definition here shows, these systems include active and multimodal perception, allowing them to perceive environmental data across multiple modes. Addressing this requires super alignment, a strategy to ensure these autonomous systems remain controllable as they scale. Super alignment moves away from external filters. It focuses on weaving ethical constraints and human objectives directly into the agents core reward logic. The goal is to make human values a foundational part of the agents reasoning process. Safety can no longer be a software patch applied to a finished product. It must be an architectural constant that operates across every agent in the society. As we bridge the gap to true autonomy, the grand challenge is building synthetic communities that inherit our values at their structural core.
